In the brackish and freshwater habitats of West Africa, the upsidedown catfish Synodontis membranaceus displays a size trajectory that has been documented through extensive field surveys. Researchers examining populations across the Niger River basin have reported that the species attains a maximum body length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range observed among congeners in the region. Sexual maturity, as determined by macroscopic inspection of gonad condition, is typically reached at a total length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters], marking the transition from the juvenile growth phase to reproductive competence. This length-based estimate of maturation aligns well with field observations of first gonadal recrudescence in seasonal floodplain populations. The difference between the size at puberty and the ultimate length suggests a substantial post-maturation growth period, a pattern common among iteroparous catfishes that continue somatic expansion well after initiating reproductive activity. Such a trajectory likely reflects an adaptive response to variable environmental conditions, allowing individuals to buffer against poor years by maintaining the capacity for future reproductive bouts while still investing in current spawning events.

Early life-history stages in Synodontis membranaceus are characterized by remarkably low initial biomass. Based on an average egg diameter of approximately one millimeter for the closely related Synodontis clarias, the calculated wet weight at birth for S. membranaceus is 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value typical of small, yolk-dependent larvae that emerge from pelagic eggs. This extraordinarily lightweight neonate faces substantial predation pressure during the planktonic larval phase, and survival hinges on rapid yolk absorption followed by the timely onset of exogenous feeding. Following eclosion from the fertilised ovum, the yolk-sac larva undergoes a period of endotrophic development that is highly sensitive to ambient temperature. Laboratory rearing trials conducted at a controlled water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] have determined that the incubation period, from gamete fusion to the hatching event, lasts approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days]. This duration is comparable to that of other tropical mochokid catfishes, though it may be extended under the cooler temperatures typical of deeper river channels.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated through fecundity analysis of gravid females, with data scaled from the well-studied congener Synodontis clarias. At a stable temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], maximum reproductive output is substantial, a finding that is corroborated by field observations of large, adherent egg masses deposited during the rainy season. Under these thermal conditions, detailed examination of ovarian tissue reveals that individual females produce approximately 115 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 115 eggs per spawning event]. This moderate clutch size, typical of many mochokids, is likely a consequence of the relatively large egg diameter and the correspondingly high energetic investment per offspring. Furthermore, field records of repeated nest attendance and observations of multiple spawning peaks within a single reproductive season indicate that females can complete up to one spawning event each day [F_R_i = up to one spawning event each day] during the brief, optimal flooding window, thereby maximizing total seasonal fecundity despite the modest per-event output.

Somatic growth following the larval period results in substantial increases in body mass as individuals progress toward the pubertal size threshold. Using the established length-weight relationship of 0.01479*L^2.92 for this species, the predicted wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 25 centimeter total length, is 49.6 grams [Wwp = 49.6 grams]. This value represents the typical body condition of a female at the onset of vitellogenesis, when energy reserves become increasingly directed toward oocyte development. The ultimate wet weight, derived from the same allometric equation applied to the 46 centimeter ultimate total length, is estimated at 309 grams [Wwi = 309 grams], a mass that positions S. membranaceus among the medium-bodied members of its genus. The transition from a pubertal mass of approximately 50 grams to an asymptotic adult mass exceeding 300 grams implies a period of sustained post-maturation growth spanning several years. This pattern is consistent with the species' life-history strategy, wherein continued somatic investment enhances individual fecundity through increased body volume and associated abdominal cavity space for egg development.

Longevity estimates for Synodontis membranaceus have been derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination in populations inhabiting Lake Chad and the upper Niger. At a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a value that aligns well with longevity data reported for the congener Synodontis clarias. This moderate lifespan, typical of many tropical freshwater siluriforms, reflects a life-history schedule in which the relatively long reproductive window is balanced against the energetic costs of maintaining a large body mass. In comparison to smaller mochokids that may live only three to four years, the decadelong potential of S. membranaceus likely facilitates a bet-hedging reproductive strategy in the face of unpredictable floodplain hydrology. The 8 year maximum longevity is also consistent with the age structure observed in exploited populations, where individuals exceeding six years are uncommon but regularly encountered in regions with low fishing pressure.
